topic: Rotator cuff muscles and glenohumeral joint capsule with cuff footprints (cadaver)

authors: Momma Daisuke, Nimura Akimoto, Muro Satoru et al.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Muscular and tendinous structures of the subscapularis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor near their insertions into the humerus (right shoulder, the acromion and coracoid process has been removed). a Anterior aspect of the shoulder. b Posterior aspect of the shoulder. CP, coracoid process; SS, scapula spine; Lat, lateral; Sup, superior
figures.what_it_shows: Right shoulder, acromion and coracoid removed: (A) anterior view of subscapularis; (B) posterior view of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor near their humeral insertions.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Outward appearance of the shoulder joint. Areas outlined by black dotted lines indicate insertions of the subscapularis (SSC), supraspinatus (SSP), infraspinatus (ISP), teres minor (TMi), and the origin of long head of triceps brachii (TRI). a Anterior aspect of the shoulder. The superior-most part of the subscapularis was left intact because it was tightly connected to the capsule and the coracohumeral ligament (red arrow). b Posterior aspect. c Superior aspect. d Inferior aspect. CP, coracoid process; SS, scapula spine; TRI, triceps; Ant, anterior; Med, medial; Lat, lateral; Sup, superior; Post, posterior
figures.what_it_shows: Glenohumeral joint capsule after removal of the cuff muscles, with dotted outlines of the insertions of SSC, SSP, ISP, TMi and origin of long head of triceps (TRI) in anterior, posterior, superior and inferior views.

key_findings: Anatomical study of 13 shoulders (9 macroscopic, 4 Thiel-embalmed for micro-CT). "On the humerus, the articular capsule was widely attached to areas without overlying rotator cuffs, with the widest width (17.3 ± 0.9 mm) attached to the axillary pouch." The inferior capsule was consistently thicker than the superior part.
clinical_relevance: The authors state that anatomical knowledge of the whole capsule is necessary to treat capsular disorders such as humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament or capsular elongation after Bankart-type instability.
notes: Excellent clean labelled photos for rotator cuff / capsule slides. Fig 4 (glenoid capsular attachment widths G1–G5) also available in the bucket if needed.

topic: Glenohumeral capsule: posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (cadaver)

authors: Nourissat Geoffroy, Bastard Claire, Cammas Claire et al.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Posterior aspect of the shoulder. ❖, posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL); ◆, intermediate capsular zone; ✪, humeral head; ✚, acromion; ★, coracoid process. (a) The posterior band of the IGHL is located under the posterior intermediate capsular zone. (b) The difference between capsule and posterior band is clearly identified. (c) Thickening of the posterior capsule defines the limit between the posterior intermediate capsular zone and the posterior band. (d) Superior view of the IGHL with posterior band. Proximal insertion is located medial to the labrum on each side of the glenoid. Distal insertion is far from the cartilage of the humeral head. (e) Posterior band of the IGHL is located medial to the labrum and distal insertion is far from the cartilage of the humeral head. key_findings: Twelve fresh cadaveric shoulders. "Concerning the PB, mean length and width were 54 ± 7 (50–60) and 16 ± 5 mm (10–25), respectively." Bands tensioned first: "in ER1, the AB at 97 ± 9° ... in IR, the PB at 64 ± 9° ... and in ABD, the PB at 87 ± 10°".
clinical_relevance: "In the case of an isolated lesion to the AB, the PB participates in anterior stabilization of the shoulder by wrapping around the humeral head" — relevant to Bankart/instability surgery.
notes: Image uses symbols instead of text labels; slide needs a legend. Only 600 px wide but sharp.

topic: Suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch (incisura scapulae) — dissection
citation: Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022 Jun 9;19(12):7065. doi: 10.3390/ijerph19127065
title: Variations in the Course and Diameter of the Suprascapular Nerve: Anatomical Study
authors: Montané-Blanchart Marta, Miguel-Pérez Maribel, Rodero-de-Lamo Lourdes et al.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Anatomical variation on left shoulder from specimen C: different anatomical structures could be observed as follows: (1) superior transverse scapular ligament; (2) inferior belly of omohyoid muscle; (3) suprascapular nerve; (4) acromioclavicular sensitive branch; (5) supraspinatus motor branch; (6) infraspinatus motor branch; note that the division into supraspinatus and infraspinatus motor branches is proximal to superior transverse scapular ligament.
figures.what_it_shows: Left shoulder (specimen C) showing the suprascapular nerve passing under the superior transverse scapular ligament, with its acromioclavicular sensory branch and supraspinatus/infraspinatus motor branches (here dividing proximal to the ligament).

key_findings: Twelve shoulders (six subjects) dissected. "In two of the six subjects, the suprascapular nerve was divided into two motor branches proximal to the superior transverse scapular ligament." Estimated diameter increase "of 2.008 mm at the suprascapular notch level and 2.047 mm at the spinoglenoid notch level".
clinical_relevance: Division of the motor branches proximal to the notch "may be relevant in the diagnosis and treatment of suprascapular neuropathy and arthroscopic procedures" (suprascapular block, notch decompression).
notes: Numbers only (1–6) in image; legend from caption. Specimen shows an anatomical variant (proximal division), so caption must say so if used as a 'normal' slide. Complements PMC4555201 already in repo.

topic: Brachial plexus trunks in the interscalene triangle / posterior triangle (cadaver)

authors: Leonhard Vanessa, Caldwell Gregory, Goh Mei et al.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Cadaveric photo illustrating the classic anatomical relationship between the scalene musculature and the trunks of the brachial plexus. In this arrangement, the superior, middle, and inferior trunks of the brachial plexus all course between the anterior and middle scalene muscle, through the interscalene gap. AS = anterior scalene; IT = inferior trunk; MS = middle scalene; MT = middle trunk; SA = subclavian artery; ST = superior trunk.

clinical_relevance: Piercing variants predispose to neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome; ultrasonography can identify them (see kesit entries for the same article).
notes: Same article also used under kesit_lecture (Fig 3) and kesit_variation (Fig 4).

topic: Deltopectoral groove: cephalic vein and deltoid branches of thoracoacromial vessels (schematic)
title: Deltoid Branch of Thoracoacromial Vein
authors: Su Ta-Wei, Wu Ching-Feng, Fu Jui-Ying et al.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Schematic of the position of cephalic and deltoid branch of thoracoacromial vein.
figures.what_it_shows: Author line drawing of the deltopectoral groove with pectoralis major cut, showing the cephalic vein and the deltoid branches of the thoracoacromial artery and vein.

key_findings: Clinical series of 802 consecutive oncology patients (intravenous port implantation). "The majority of patients (93.6%) could be identified as thoracoacromial vessel. The deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial vein is located on the medial aspect of the deltopectoral groove beneath the pectoralis major muscle (85.8%) and in the deep part of the deltopectoral groove (14.2%)."
clinical_relevance: "It is a safe alternative entry vessel for intravenous port implantation" when the cephalic vein is not usable.
notes: Not a cadaver study (intra-operative clinical series); Fig 1 is an intra-operative photo and was not taken. Schematic is the authors' own (no reproduction note).

topic: Axillary nerve under the deltoid: acromio-axillary distance and safe zone (regio deltoidea)

authors: Patra Apurba, Singh Manjit, Kaur Harsimarjit et al.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: The deltoid muscle was replaced in its original anatomical position. The course of axillary nerve is shown with the help of needles, and the anterior acromio-axillary distance (AD) and posterior acromioaxillary distance (PD) were measured. AEA, anterior edge of acromion; PEA, posterior edge of acromion.
figures.what_it_shows: Deltoid replaced in position; course of the axillary nerve marked with pins and the anterior/posterior acromio-axillary distances drawn from the acromial edges.

key_findings: Sixty shoulders of thirty cadavers. "The mean of anterior and posterior AA distance was 5.22 cm and 4.17 cm, respectively." "The minimum AA distance was found to be 3.50 cm. So this should be considered as the maximum permissible length of the deltoid split."
clinical_relevance: Defines a safe area for deltoid-splitting approaches; the axillary nerve's anterior branch is at particular risk of iatrogenic injury.
notes: LICENCE CC BY-NC (flag). Fig 1 (inner deltoid surface) had no labels and was not kept.

topic: Dorsal scapular artery origin and its relation to the brachial plexus (scapular anastomosis)
title: Origin variations and brachial plexus relationship of the dorsal scapular artery
authors: Lai Kuen-Cherng, Ho Han-Chen

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Representative images showing the relationships of the brachial plexus and arteries. (a) Dorsal scapular artery (*) is a branch of the transverse cervical artery (TCA), which arises from the thyrocervical trunk (T). The above arteries pass over the brachial plexus towards the back. The suprascapular artery (●) passing through the brachial plexus is a branch of the axillary artery. AS: anterior scalene muscle; I: inferior trunk; M: middle trunk; S: superior trunk of brachial plexus; SA: subclavian artery. (b) Dorsal scapular artery (*) passing through the middle (M) and inferior (I) trunks of the brachial plexus is a direct branch from the second part of the subclavian artery (SA).
figures.what_it_shows: (a) Dorsal scapular artery (*) from the transverse cervical artery passing over the trunks; (b) DSA (*) passing between the plexus trunks when arising directly from the subclavian artery.

key_findings: 79 sides of 41 cadavers. "the dorsal scapular artery originated most frequently from the transverse cervical artery (48%), followed by the direct branch from the third part (25%) and the second part (22%) of the subclavian artery and from the axillary artery (5%)." "Only 3% of the dorsal scapular artery passed through the brachial plexus if its origin was the transverse cervical artery" vs "100% and 75%" for second/third-part origins.
clinical_relevance: Variations matter for "supraclavicular brachial plexus block and head and neck reconstruction with pedicled or free flaps."
notes: Original series with prevalence; good for scapular anastomosis lecture.

topic: Ectopic insertion of pectoralis minor tendon over the coracoid (pectoralis minor variants)

figures.label: Fig 2
figures.caption: Exemplary photograph of a right shoulder seen from superior.The ectopic pectoralis minor tendon (*) runs over the coracoid process and through the branches of the coracoacromial ligament (CAL). A = acromion, CAL = coracoacromial ligament, CP = coracoid process, H = humerus, PMM = pectoralis minor muscle.
figures.what_it_shows: Right shoulder from superior: ectopic pectoralis minor tendon (*) crossing the coracoid and passing through the coracoacromial ligament towards the humerus.

figures.label: Fig 3
figures.caption: Right EIPMT (A and A’) and normal (B and B’) type shoulder from cranial (A and B) and lateral (A’ and B’).Insertion areas are marked on the coracoid process. Red = PMM, black = CAL, blue = CHL, * medial CHL fibers, violet = CGL, green = coracobrachialis muscle/short head of biceps. key_findings: 45 shoulders dissected. "The prevalence of PMM variations was 37.84%." "Shoulders with variations showed a statistically significant smaller coracopectoral distance (p<0.001) and larger insertion areas (p<0.003)".

notes: Fig 1 of this paper is 'Modified from Lee 2014' and was NOT taken. Fig 3 has no text labels (colour code only).

key_findings: Review of shoulder anatomy and normal variants on radiography, MRI, MR/CT arthrography. Labrum "may appear thickened and cordlike ... as in the Buford complex ... or completely absent in 30% of healthy subjects" (MGHL).
clinical_relevance: Normal variants must be recognised to avoid misdiagnosis as pathology (labral tear, fracture, osteophyte).
notes: Arrow-based labels; anatomical names only on schematic (A of g16). Same article used in kesit_variation.

topic: Normal variants on imaging: os acromiale (CT) and anterosuperior labral variants incl. Buford complex (MR arthrography)
citation: J Belg Soc Radiol. 2017 Dec 16;101(Suppl 2):3. doi: 10.5334/jbr-btr.1467
title: Shoulder Anatomy and Normal Variants
authors: Kadi Redouane, Milants Annemieke, Shahabpour Maryam
journal: Journal of the Belgian Society of Radiology

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Os acromiale. Axial CT arthrography through the acromioclavicular joint demonstrates an os acromiale (arrow) with synchondrosis (arrowhead). An os acromiale should not be confused with a fracture fragment and the synchondrosis with a pseudarthrosis. In this case, there is a communication between the synchondrosis and the glenohumeral joint (with high-density contrast penetration), which is not normal. Subchondral cystic changes are also seen in the zone of pseudarthrosis.
figures.what_it_shows: Axial CT arthrogram through the AC joint: os acromiale (arrow) with synchondrosis (arrowhead).

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Schematic illustration of the normal capsulolabral complex and anatomical variations. They are shown on a lateral view onto the glenoid. (a) Normal anatomy; (b) Sublabral recess (sublabral sulcus); (c) Sublabral foramen (sublabral hole); (d) Buford complex. LHBT: long head of biceps tendon, SGHL: superior glenohumeral ligament, MGHL: middle glenohumeral ligament, IGHL: inferior glenohumeral ligament.
figures.what_it_shows: Lateral view of the glenoid: (a) normal capsulolabral complex; (b) sublabral recess; (c) sublabral foramen; (d) Buford complex.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Buford complex. (A) Axial PD-weighted and (B) Sagittal fat-suppressed T1-weighted MR arthrographic images show a cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament (white arrow) associated with an absent anterior superior labrum (black arrow) mimicking a labral tear with normal posterior labrum. Subscapularis tendon (arrowhead). (Courtesy of Dr Henri Guerini).
figures.what_it_shows: Buford complex: cord-like MGHL (white arrow) with absent anterosuperior labrum (black arrow) on axial and sagittal MR arthrograms.

key_findings: "The incidence of this variant [os acromiale] can reach up to 15% of the population"; the anterosuperior labrum/MGHL may be cord-like as in the Buford complex.
clinical_relevance: "An os acromiale should not be confused with a fracture fragment and the synchondrosis with a pseudarthrosis"; Buford complex mimics a labral tear.
notes: Review article without original prevalence. Fig 15 caption ends '(Courtesy of Dr Henri Guerini)' — published under the article's CC BY, but flag third-party image origin; prefer g12 + g9 if in doubt. Fig 14 (sublabral foramen) is also 'Courtesy of' and was not taken.

topic: Os acromiale prevalence on MRI (3697 shoulder MRIs) and coexistence with rotator cuff tears
citation: Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc. 2026 Feb 19;60:e25714. doi: 10.5152/j.aott.2026.25714
title: Prevalence of os acromiale and concomitant rotator cuff tears: a focused assessment of 3697 shoulder magnetic resonance imagings
authors: Birsel Olgar, Yığman Gizem Timoçin, Günerbüyük Caner et al.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Os acromiale visualized on T2-weighted axial (A) and T1-weighted sagittal oblique (B) MR images. The unfused ossification center (white arrow) creates a double acromioclavicular joint appearance characteristic of os acromiale.
figures.what_it_shows: Os acromiale on T2 axial (A) and T1 sagittal oblique (B): unfused ossification centre producing a 'double AC joint' appearance (arrow).

key_findings: 3697 shoulder MRIs. "Os acromiale was identified in 26 cases, corresponding to a prevalence of 0.7%. Only 11 cases were mentioned in the original radiology reports." "Subtypes included 12 preacromion, 13 mesoacromion, and 1 metaacromion." Rotator cuff tears in "20 of 26 patients with os acromiale (77%)".
clinical_relevance: Focused evaluation "documented more cases than routine radiology reports, underscoring the added value of targeted assessment."
notes: LICENCE CC BY-NC (flag). Panel A is very dark; panel B is the useful one.

topic: Os acromiale in a general population MRI cohort (SHIP, 3050 participants) — type scheme
title: Os acromiale: prevalence and associated patient-related factors—a population-based study of three thousand and fifty participants
authors: Fischer Cornelius Sebastian, Floß Matthias, Ittermann Till et al.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Scheme showing the types of os acromiale: pre-acromion, meso-acromion, meta-acromion, and basi-acromion
figures.what_it_shows: Outline scheme of the acromion ossification centres: pre-, meso-, meta- and basi-acromion.

key_findings: "In total, 1.9% (58/3050) had an os acromiale, while 21 were unilateral left, 23 were unilateral right, and 14 were bilateral. Sixty-eight meso-acromions, three pre-acromions, and one meta-acromion were detected." More frequent in men.

topic: Anterosuperior labral variants (sublabral recess, sublabral foramen, Buford complex): meta-analysis
title: Prevalence of the anterosuperior capsulolabral anatomical variations and their association with pathologies of the glenoid labrum: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Benes Michal, Kachlik David, Kopp Lubomir et al.
journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Schematic drawings of the sublabral recess (A), the sublabral foramen (B), and the Buford complex (C). CLMGHL cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament, GL glenoid labrum, LHBBM long head of the biceps brachii muscle, SSM subscapularis muscle
figures.what_it_shows: Three drawings of the glenoid showing (A) sublabral recess, (B) sublabral foramen, (C) Buford complex with cord-like MGHL.

key_findings: 20 studies, 7601 upper limbs. Pooled prevalence: sublabral recess "57.2% (95% CI 30.0–84.4%)", sublabral foramen "13.5% (95% CI 8.2–18.9%)", Buford complex "3.0% (95% CI 1.5–4.5)"; "individuals with Buford complex have RR 2.4 (95% CI 1.3–4.7) of developing SLAP lesions".
clinical_relevance: Differentiating these variants from pathology avoids unnecessary iatrogenic complications; Buford complex "may be a predisposing factor for sustaining a SLAP lesion."
notes: Schematic only 669x193 (three panels ~220 px each) — small; usable as a strip. Pooled data mix arthroscopy, MRI and cadaver studies.

topic: Brachial plexus piercing variants of the anterior scalene on ultrasound (and cadaver prevalence)
title: Ultrasonographic Diagnosis of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome Secondary to Brachial Plexus Piercing Variation
authors: Leonhard Vanessa, Caldwell Gregory, Goh Mei et al.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: The superior piercing variant, the most common brachial plexus variant, identified using ultrasonography in the present study: (A) unlabeled; and (B) labeled. Note that the superior trunk is not separated from the anterior scalene in this condition, visible as a lack of hyperechoic fascia. AS = anterior scalene; IT = inferior trunk; MS = middle scalene; MT = middle trunk; SCM = sternocleidomastoid; ST = superior trunk. The green outlines demarcate the trunks of the brachial plexus.
figures.what_it_shows: Superior piercing variant on US, unlabeled (A) and labelled (B): superior trunk not separated from the anterior scalene.

key_findings: Cadaver part: 82 necks, "In 62.1%, C5, superior trunk, or superior + middle trunks pierced the anterior scalene." US screening of 22 subjects (44 plexuses): "Eight of these were classified as piercing variants ... (18.2%)"; superior piercing "n = 4; 9.1%", multiple piercing "n = 3; 6.8%", C5 piercing "n = 1; 2.3%". nTOS symptoms in 50% of piercing variants vs 13.9% of normal plexuses.
clinical_relevance: "The addition of ultrasonography to nTOS diagnosis, especially for patients with BP branching variation, would allow clinicians to visualize and identify atypical patient anatomy."
notes: Two-panel US image 716 px wide; labels small but legible. Fig 2 (cadaver variants A–C) is also in the bucket if a topo slide is wanted.
